initial_presentation: A 22-year-old woman arrived at the emergency department with generalized weakness, vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, a 40-lb weight loss, and severe intermittent headaches over the past 2 days. She had previously undergone evaluation over the last 3 months for episodes of fainting, abdominal pain, vomiting, and chronic constipation. In the 2 weeks before her hospitalization, her mother reported episodes of right-sided weakness and facial droop.

A 3-month-old male infant presented with bilateral corneal opacity present since birth and was referred from the pediatric unit for ophthalmic evaluation. The mother, aged 35 years at the time of childbirth, is HIV positive. Prenatal and natal history were otherwise unremarkable. There is no family history of similar ocular conditions or other congenital anomalies. Initial ophthalmic examination revealed a positive light pursuit and homogeneous bilateral central corneal opacity without neovascularization.

A 13-year-old female presented to the outpatient department of a tertiary care hospital in Karachi with a two-day history of sudden onset of restless, abnormal movements. These movements initially appeared in both upper limbs, then spread to the trunk on the same day, and eventually involved both lower limbs by the second day. The patient's mother noted that these movements interfered with daily activities such as bathing, picking up utensils, and eating. No abnormal movements were observed during sleep. The patient had a history of sore throat and fever three weeks prior, which resolved on its own. General physical examination was normal. The patient was alert and oriented to place and time but appeared anxious and restless with involuntary movements while lying down. Vital signs were recorded as heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 22/min, afebrile, and blood pressure 105/80 mmHg. Mild anemia was noted. Examination revealed unclear speech, difficulty walking, generalized hypotonia, and irregular muscle contractions and relaxations, including pronation of the forearm on an outstretched hand above her head, known as 'Milkmaid's sign.'

Family 1406 is a consanguineous family from Colombia. The proband, a 21-year-old male, first presented with an unusual stiff-legged gait at about one year of age. His pediatrician found no concerning features in his developmental history or examination at that time. As he grew, his parents observed that he would not bend his knees when jumping, and his gait would occasionally become stiff-legged. A neurologist noted good reflexes and no weakness. Over time, his symptoms worsened. He participated in soccer and other sports but was slower than his peers. He reported no difficulty initiating movements; however, after running for several yards, he experienced sudden muscle stiffness in his legs, requiring him to stop and rest. After a brief rest, he could resume running without difficulty. The stiffness was not accompanied by pain or weakness but worsened with cold exposure. He also experienced difficulty releasing a lacrosse or hockey stick after gripping it for a length of time and reported jaw stiffness with prolonged chewing, without choking or dysphagia. Neither parent had muscle symptoms. At 16 years, physical examination showed eyelid, hand, and foot myotonia with mild percussion myotonia at the thenar eminences and the extensor digitorum communis. At 20 years, physical examination showed eyelid myotonia and mild grip myotonia, with no percussion myotonia. Strength was normal in all extremities, with no muscle hypertrophy or atrophy and no heel cord contractures.

A 27-year-old man, previously healthy, has experienced two years of subcutaneous nodules distributed across his body, excluding the head, neck, hands, and feet. The nodules appeared gradually and increased in number over time. The patient reported paresthesia and significant pain that disrupted daily activities, which did not respond to analgesics or anti-inflammatory medications. There was no history of mental disorders, and the systemic review was unremarkable. The patient had no family history of obesity and did not consume alcohol or smoke. Physical examination revealed multiple soft-tissue swellings, predominantly on the trunk and upper limbs, with sparing of the face, hands, and feet. These swellings were painless upon palpation. The patient's BMI was 24 kg/m2. Neurological examination was normal, and other physical findings were unremarkable.

A 20-year-old Caucasian woman, with no prior medical history, arrived at the emergency room with numbness and weakness in her left-sided limbs. Neurologic examination showed no cranial nerve deficits and 4/5 strength in the left-sided limbs. There was no evidence of cerebellar dysfunction. She was unable to localize tactile stimuli or judge the size and shape of objects. Sensations of pain, pressure, and temperature were intact.
A 66-year-old male presented with left nasal congestion, left periorbital swelling, and mild proptosis that began one month ago.
A 62-year-old male with a history of being overweight, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with a hemoglobin level of 20.4 g/dL and a hematocrit of 0.59.
A 68-year-old male was admitted to the hospital due to fever, cough, and progressive shortness of breath for 10 days.
A 79-year-old woman with a history of cerebral infarction in the left basal ganglia presented with headache and dizziness.
